title: Feasibility Ordering of Entanglement-Source Placement for Qubit Channels
abstract: This work studies the placement of an entanglement source along a communication line formed by two noisy qubit channels. Recent work argued, on analytical and numerical grounds, that midpoint placement should be at least as favorable as endpoint placement. Here it is shown that, for arbitrary qubit channels, if a sequential composition can preserve entanglement, then the corresponding parallel action cannot annihilate all entanglement. The proof uses the transpose-factorization criterion introduced in that recent work. Quantum Sinkhorn scaling converts every strictly positive qubit channel into a unital representative, and the special normal form of unital qubit channels then yields the required factorization of the transposed map through the original channel. Depolarizing regularization and the closedness of the set of entanglement-breaking channels extend the result to arbitrary channels. Consequently, $Λ_1 \otimes Λ_2 \in \mathrm{EA}$ implies $Λ_2 \circ Λ_1 \in \mathrm{EB}$, and, by exchanging the two channels, the same holds for the opposite composition order. This proves the recent conjecture that midpoint placement is optimal for all qubit channels, in the feasibility sense in which that optimality was originally defined.
summary: This paper proves a fundamental relationship between the entanglement properties of parallel versus sequential compositions of noisy qubit channels. Specifically, it shows that if the parallel combination is entanglement-assisted, the sequential composition must be entanglement-breaking. This establishes the optimality of midpoint placement for entanglement sources in the feasibility sense.
main_problem: The paper investigates the feasibility ordering of placing an entanglement source when considering two noisy qubit channels ($\Lambda_1 \otimes \Lambda_2$ vs. $\Lambda_2 \circ \Lambda_1$).
main_result: It proves that if the parallel composition of two qubit channels is entanglement-assisted (EA), then the corresponding sequential composition must be entanglement-breaking (EB), establishing midpoint optimality in the feasibility sense.
method: The proof utilizes the transpose-factorization criterion, extending results from strictly positive channels to arbitrary channels via depolarizing regularization and quantum Sinkhorn scaling.
model_or_system: The system involves two noisy qubit channels ($\Lambda_1, \Lambda_2$) acting on qubits, analyzed through concepts like entanglement breaking (EB) and entanglement assisting (EA).
key_observables: Entanglement-Breaking (EB) and Entanglement-Assisted (EA) properties of channel compositions ($\Lambda_1 \otimes \Lambda_2$ and $\Lambda_2 \circ \Lambda_1$).
important_parameters: The channels $\Lambda_1$ and $\Lambda_2$, and the concept of strict positivity for initial factorization steps.
main_assumptions: The extension of the factorization criterion from strictly positive channels to arbitrary channels relies on depolarizing regularization.
paper_structure: The paper develops the argument by first establishing the necessary transpose factorization for strictly positive channels using Quantum Sinkhorn scaling, and then extending this result to arbitrary channels using regularization techniques to prove the main implication.
why_interesting: This work provides rigorous mathematical tools (like factorization criteria and regularization) to compare different physical arrangements of quantum resources (entanglement sources) in open quantum systems.
